intro: The line between AI as tool and AI as collaborator blurred further this week, with a Stanford physicist crediting GPT-6 Astra as a key contributor to an 83-page quantum gravity paper — a claim that has the physics community both intrigued and deeply skeptical. Meanwhile, the geopolitics of AI hardware heated up as Nvidia froze server shipments across Southeast Asia, and on the consumer side, Google is betting that everyday users want to *build* with AI, not just chat with it. It's a day that captures the full spectrum of where AI sits right now: from the edges of theoretical physics to your Pixel home screen.

stories.title: Framework urges picking one personal AI experiment per week instead of chasing vague ambition
stories.summary: The article argues most AI advice fails because it tells people to be ambitious without specifying about what. It proposes a four-step framework: find something worth an evening based on existing interests, let AI handle setup while you do the interesting work, meet people through the activity, then honestly evaluate whether it deserves a second evening — each step with a copy-paste prompt.
stories.opinion: A refreshingly grounded counterpoint to the relentless 'be more ambitious with AI' drumbeat. The 'tyranny of the text box' framing is memorable and accurate.

stories.title: Nvidia pauses server shipments to Southeast Asia amid U.S. export-rule crackdown on China workaround
stories.summary: Nvidia told Dell and Super Micro to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia while it checks regional partners' compliance with U.S. export rules. The pause follows Commerce Department action closing a loophole that let Chinese firms remotely access Nvidia AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers, which the Institute for Progress estimates supply roughly 24% of China's AI computing power.
stories.opinion: A significant escalation in the chip-export saga that could disrupt Southeast Asian data-center buildouts and further squeeze China's access to frontier AI compute.

stories.title: Stanford physicist credits GPT-6 Astra in 83-page quantum gravity preprint, drawing praise and skepticism
stories.summary: Stanford physicist Venkatesa Chandrasekaran published an 83-page preprint proposing a quantum theory of gravity, crediting OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra with helping develop calculations over months using roughly 400 million tokens. The paper uses light paths through spacetime to describe gravity at the quantum level and claims to avoid standard infinities, but only covers empty space. It has drawn praise from Sam Altman and skepticism from physicists who question the AI-assisted methodology; it remains unreviewed.
stories.opinion: The most concrete test case yet for whether AI can meaningfully contribute to frontier theoretical physics — but the lack of peer review and the publicity circus around it make it hard to judge the actual science.

stories.title: Android's Gemini-powered 'Create My Widget' beta lets Pixel users vibe-code custom widgets
stories.summary: Android's new 'Create My Widget' beta, announced at Google I/O and rolling out to Pixel phones in November 2026, lets users create custom home screen widgets via natural language prompts powered by Gemini AI. The Verge found it fun for simple tasks like rotating movie quotes but inadequate for complex data-dependent tasks like real-time bus arrivals.
stories.opinion: A lightweight but telling example of vibe-coding reaching mainstream consumer products — useful for novelty, not yet for anything you'd actually rely on.

tweet_headlines.author: crazyMLguy
tweet_headlines.headline: ISTA-DASLab squeezed Inkling-2-Mini down to __11.43 GB at 3.5 bpw__ while retaining 99.2% of its original task performance.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Inkling-2-Mini now fits into just 11.43 GB with 99.2% of its original performance

ISTA-DASLab has released new GSQ-RCO quantized versions of Inkling-2-Mini, bringing a 26.4B sparse MoE model down to just 2.75–3.5 bits per weight.

Key highlights:

3.5 bpw: 11.43 GB model size.

Retains 99.2% of the base model's task average.

Within 1 point of the original across all tested benchmarks.

Supports a massive 1M-token context window.

Runs as standard GGUF in llama.cpp.

Impressive result: aggressive quantization without sacrificing much reasoning and coding performance.

Models: https://t.co/5QgRyrazAs

Eval: https://t.co/zvfXKxg5JY

tweet_headlines.author: alex_prompter
tweet_headlines.headline: Google's prompting guide tucks away __a tested system instruction that makes Gemini plan before it acts__ — researchers say it improved results.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Google has a tested system prompt that makes Gemini plan before it acts.

You can ask Gemini 4 Neon to turn it into your own custom assistant.

It's tucked away at the bottom of Google's prompting guide. Google says its researchers tested it on tasks where the AI has to follow a complex rulebook and deal with a real user, and it improved results.

Send this prompt to Gemini 4 Neon 👇

<context>Google's prompting guide for Gemini includes a system instruction its researchers tested to make Gemini plan before it acts. It's in the "Agentic workflows" section of https://t.co/78DZbDxd3Y</context>
<task>
Read that system instruction. Then ask me 5 questions about one job I hand off often, like answering customer emails, planning projects or checking contracts. Then adapt Google's 9 rules to that job:
1. Keep the rules that matter for it and cut the ones that don't.
2. Swap Google's general wording for my real rules, risks and tools.
3. Add the moments where it must stop and ask me before it acts.
Then build it as custom instructions I can paste into a Gem.
</task>
<rules>Keep Google's core idea of planning before every action. Show the original rule next to each change. Don't invent business rules I didn't give you.</rules>
<output>The finished Gem instructions, ready to paste, and 3 test requests I can run to check it works.</output>
<input>The job I want to hand off [ ]</input>

tweet_headlines.author: jundotkim
tweet_headlines.headline: oMLX 0.8.4 ships __LoopCD decoding for Inkling 2 Mini__, boosting prefill speeds by up to 124% and decode rates by up to 121% at 128K context.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
oMLX 0.8.4 is out!
Inkling 2 Mini got much faster and gets LoopCD decoding, and DeepSeek V4.1 decodes faster with several requests at once. 
https://t.co/t9pHL0naGu

Faster @thinkymachines Inkling 2 Mini (oQ4e, Lightning MTP on, M5 Ultra)
- Prefill: 3,668 -> 5,664 tok/s at 16K (+54%), and up to +124% at 128K
- Decode (Greedy): 129.0 -> 208.6 tok/s at 4K (+62%), and 57.4 -> 126.5 tok/s at 128K (+121%)
- Decode (Sampling): 113.1 -> 160.2 tok/s (+42%), and 56.2 -> 112.1 tok/s at 128K (+100%)
- Lightning MTP now runs for concurrent requests too. 8 requests decode 225.3 -> 380.2 tok/s in total (+69%), and 2 requests get +161%.

LoopCD for Inkling 2 Mini
- A new decoding option from "Decoding Looped Transformers Better for (Almost) Free" by @onloglogn and co-authors. It compares the last loop pass with the first one when picking each token, with no training and no extra model.
- ARC-Challenge: 69.62% -> 71.93%, HumanEval: 152 -> 155 of 164
- Turn it on in Model Settings > Experimental Features. It's off by default and costs 9-13% decode speed.

Faster DeepSeek V4.1 (oQ2.5h, Lightning MTP on, M5 Ultra)
- 4 requests decode 113.5 -> 140.3 tok/s in total (+24%), and 2 and 8 requests get +10% and +12%.
- On tensor-parallel clusters, a short request during a 64K prefill gets its first token in 7.4 s instead of 59.3 s.

Also in 0.8.4
- Inkling 2 experts can stay on SSD. On a 24 GB Mac memory goes 17.0 -> 10.2 GB, and a 14.8K prompt that ran out of memory now runs.
- Hy4 Flash decodes 43.5 -> 56.0 tok/s with Lightning MTP on a cached 17K prompt (+29%).
- Splash now serves Inkling 2 Mini, with image input.

70 PRs merged since 0.8.3. Thanks to the 43 contributors in this release, and a warm welcome to the 19 first-time contributors!

I've always said oMLX should let a friend who bought a MacBook only yesterday enjoy local AI today. Watching the open source community's work bring it closer every day makes me really happy!

tweet_headlines.headline: __6.5 hours of free Anthropic courses__, taken in this sequence, gets you from zero to building MCP tools and running evals on Claude.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
6.5 hours of free Anthropic courses is enough to build your own tools on Claude, if you take them in this order:

1. Claude Platform 101 (1.5 hr)
2. Tool use with the Messages API (1.5 hr)
3. Introduction to Model Context Protocol (1 hr)
4. Model Context Protocol: Advanced topics (1.5 hr)
5. Introduction to evals (1 hr)

I put them in this order because if you skip step 2 then step 3 makes no sense, and if you skip step 3 then step 4 is guesswork.

It's all free, and you can start on Claude Academy.
